title: From Data to Decisions: Your First Predictive Model
subtitle: What predictive analytics is, why every business question about the future is a prediction problem — and a churn model you build yourself before 7:30

objectives.title: Locate Prediction on the Analytics Map
objectives.description: Descriptive tells you what happened. Predictive tells you what will happen next — and to whom. Prescriptive decides what to do about it. This course lives in the middle, and feeds the third.

objectives.title: Walk the Prediction Lifecycle
objectives.description: Business question → data → features → model → evaluation → decision → monitoring. You'll learn the loop tonight and repeat it thirteen times, on thirteen datasets, until it's reflex.

objectives.title: Build a Churn Model in Twelve Lines
objectives.description: The IBM Telco dataset: 7,043 customers, 20 columns, one question — who leaves next month? pandas to load, scikit-learn to fit, a held-out test set to keep you honest.

objectives.title: Discover Why Accuracy Lies
objectives.description: A model that predicts 'nobody churns' is 73% accurate on this data. Yours must beat that — and you'll learn the first three questions to ask of any accuracy number.

agenda.title: Welcome & The Course Ahead
agenda.description: Introductions, what predictive analytics is, and the semester arc: data and features, regression, classification and decisions, trees and gradient boosting, evaluation and trust, unsupervised learning, forecasting, neural networks and LLM features, and finally shipping a model.
bulletPoints: Every session: a business question → a dataset → a model you build → an evaluation you can defend → a decision
Grading: labs 15% · homework 25% · midterm model competition 20% · final prediction story 40%

agenda.title: The Prediction Lifecycle
agenda.description: From CRISP-DM to the modern ML loop. The step business people skip is framing: what exactly is being predicted, for whom, how far ahead, and what decision changes if the prediction is right?
bulletPoints: Netflix, Capital One, and your local hospital all run the same seven-step loop — only the data changes
Prediction unit, horizon, and decision: write these three down before you touch a keyboard

agenda.title: Meet the Data: Telco Customer Churn
agenda.description: 7,043 customers of a telecom company. Tenure, contract type, monthly charges, internet service, tech support — and a Churn column that says whether they left last month. Ten minutes of pandas to know it before we model it.
bulletPoints: 26.5% of customers churned — that number is your first baseline
Month-to-month contracts churn at 43%; two-year contracts at 3%. The signal is already visible

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, coffee, meet a future competition teammate.

agenda.title: Your First Model, Live
agenda.description: Split the data, fit a logistic regression on a handful of features, predict on the customers the model has never seen. Twelve lines of Python, and a probability of churn for every customer.
bulletPoints: train_test_split with stratify=y — the single most important line in the notebook
fit on train, predict on test, never the other way around: the discipline that separates analysts from fortune-tellers

agenda.title: Why Accuracy Lies
agenda.description: Our model scores 79% accuracy. The 'nobody churns' model scores 73%. Is 80 good? We open the confusion matrix and discover the model catches only half of the churners — and that a retention offer costs $50 while a lost customer costs $1,500.
bulletPoints: Three questions for any accuracy: compared with what baseline? on which data? at what cost per mistake?
Preview of Session 6: the same model, a different threshold, $200K more profit

activities.title: Your First Predictive Model: Who Churns Next Month?
activities.description: A telecom company has 7,043 customers and knows which ones left last month. Build a model that scores every customer's probability of leaving — then judge it honestly against the do-nothing baseline.

steps.title: Frame the prediction
steps.description: Unit: one customer. Target: Churn (Yes/No). Horizon: next month. Decision: who gets a retention offer. Write these four down at the top of the notebook — they're the contract with the business.

steps.title: Look before you model
steps.description: Churn rate overall (26.5%), then by contract type, by tenure bucket, by internet service. If a chart shows no signal, no model will find it either.

steps.title: Split, fit, predict
steps.description: Hold out 20% with stratify=y. Fit a logistic regression on tenure, monthly charges, and contract type. Predict probabilities for the held-out customers.

steps.title: Judge it honestly
steps.description: Accuracy versus the 73% baseline, then the confusion matrix: how many churners did we catch, how many loyal customers did we bother? Sketch what a $50 offer and a $1,500 lost customer do to the answer.

codeBlock.code:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, confusion_matrix

url = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harslan/isom-835/master/public/data/telco_churn.csv'
df = pd.read_csv(url)

X = pd.get_dummies(df[['tenure', 'MonthlyCharges', 'Contract']], drop_first=True)
y = (df['Churn'] == 'Yes').astype(int)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=835)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = model.predict(X_test)

print(f'Baseline (nobody churns): {1 - y_test.mean():.1%}')
print(f'Model accuracy:           {accuracy_score(y_test, pred):.1%}')
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, pred))

activities.discussionNote: Notice what the split gives you that a spreadsheet cannot: an honest score. The model never saw the 1,409 test customers, so its 79% is a forecast of how it will do on next month's customers — not a memory of last month's. And notice what accuracy hides: the bottom-left cell of that matrix is churners we missed, each one worth $1,500. Session 6 is about that cell.

takeaways.text: Predictive analytics sits between describing the past and prescribing the future: descriptive → predictive → prescriptive. A prediction is only valuable when a decision changes because of it.

The loop is always the same: frame → data → features → model → evaluate → decide → monitor. The framing step (unit, target, horizon, decision) is the one business people skip and the one that matters most.
Accuracy lies. Always ask: compared with what baseline, on which held-out data, and at what cost per mistake? A 'nobody churns' model is 73% accurate and worth nothing.
